questions.question: From the alternatives given below, choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'the chattering classes'.

options.text: A person who talks idly and actively about someone or something
An academic course that is not at all demanding or challenging
Educated individuals known for frequently discussing and commenting on current events, such as politics, perhaps in the media
Someone who talks constantly or excessively, especially about trivial or irrelevant things

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Educated individuals known for frequently discussing and commenting on current events, such as politics, perhaps in the media**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom **'the chattering classes'** refers to educated, middle-class people who enjoy discussing social, political, and cultural issues, often seen as having opinions but not necessarily taking action. (प्रबुद्ध और मुखर वर्ग)
 
 
• **Example: **The proposed changes to the education system were met with mixed reviews from **the chattering classes** in the national newspapers.
 
 
 
• **'Educated individuals known for frequently discussing and commenting on current events, such as politics, perhaps in the media'** perfectly describes this group of people who are often journalists, academics, or commentators. (शिक्षित वर्ग जो अक्सर राजनीति जैसी समसामयिक घटनाओं पर चर्चा और टिप्पणी करने के लिए जाना जाता है)
 
 
• **Example: **While the working class focused on their daily wages, **the chattering classes** were preoccupied with the intricacies of international diplomacy.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the correct meaning of the idiom is related to a specific social group that engages in intellectual discussion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Educated individuals known for frequently discussing and commenting on current events, such as politics, perhaps in the media**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **A person who talks idly and actively about someone or something** (गपशप करने वाला व्यक्ति): Someone who engages in rumors or casual talk about the private affairs of others.
 
 
• **Example:** Being a **gossip**, he was the first to spread the news about the neighbor's secret wedding.
 
 
 
• **An academic course that is not at all demanding or challenging** (एक अत्यंत सरल शैक्षणिक पाठ्यक्रम): Often colloquially referred to as a 'bird course' or 'gut course'.
 
 
• **Example:** Most students signed up for the elective because it was known as a **cake-walk course** with no final exam.
 
 
 
• **Someone who talks constantly or excessively, especially about trivial or irrelevant things** (बहुत अधिक बोलने वाला/बकवादी): A person who talks a lot without saying much of importance.
 
 
• **Example:** The man sitting next to me on the bus was a real **chatterbox** and didn't stop talking about his cats for the whole hour.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
Will the necessary arrangements be made by the organisers before the festival starts?

options.text: Do the organisers make the necessary arrangements before the festival starts?
Will the organisers make the necessary arrangements before the festival starts?
Have the organisers made the necessary arrangements before the festival starts?
Did the organisers make the necessary arrangements before the festival starts?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Will the organisers make the necessary arrangements before the festival starts?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The given sentence is in the **Passive Voice** and follows the structure of an **Interrogative Sentence** in the **Future Indefinite Tense** (Simple Future).

• The passive construction for simple future interrogative is: **Will/Shall + Object + be + V3 (Past Participle) + by + Subject?**. Here, the object is **the necessary arrangements** and the subject (agent) is **the organisers**.

• To convert this into **Active Voice**, the structure must change to: **Will/Shall + Subject + V1 (Base Form) + Object?**.

• Applying this rule, the subject **the organisers** moves to the beginning after the auxiliary verb **Will**, and the main verb **made** reverts to its base form **make**.

• The phrase **before the festival starts** is a subordinate clause that remains unchanged during the voice transformation.

• Therefore, the active form is: **Will the organisers make the necessary arrangements before the festival starts?**.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Active vs. Passive Voice Rules:**

• **Active Voice:** The subject performs the action (e.g., **The organisers will make...**).

• **Passive Voice:** The subject receives the action (e.g., **Arrangements will be made...**).

• In **Future Indefinite**, the auxiliary **will** is accompanied by **be** in the passive form, while the main verb always takes the **third form (V3)**.

• Options using **Do**, **Have**, or **Did** are incorrect because they change the **Tense** of the sentence to **Simple Present**, **Present Perfect**, and **Simple Past** respectively.

• The auxiliary verb **Will** is used for third-person plural subjects like **the organisers** in modern English standard usage.

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
The gate must not be left open by anyone.

options.text: No one should be leaving the gate open.
No one must leave the gate open.
The gate must not stay open.
Keep the gate not open by anyone.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**No one must leave the gate open.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence is in the **Passive Voice**, structured as: **Object (The gate)** + **Modal (must)** + **Negative (not)** + **be** + **Past Participle (left)** + **Complement (open)** + **Preposition (by)** + **Agent (anyone)**.

• To transform a sentence into the **Active Voice**, the **agent** of the passive sentence (**anyone**) becomes the **subject** of the active sentence. In English grammar, when a negative statement involves **not + anyone**, it is conventionally expressed using the negative pronoun **No one** or **Nobody** as the subject.

• The **Modal Verb (must)** denotes a strong obligation or a strict prohibition. During voice conversion, the **modal verb** must remain unchanged to preserve the original **mood** and **intensity** of the instruction.

• In **Active Voice** constructions with modals, the auxiliary **be** is removed, and the **Past Participle (V3)** form of the verb (**left**) is converted back to its **Base Form (V1)**, which is **leave**.

• The resulting **Active Voice** structure follows the pattern: **Subject (No one)** + **Modal (must)** + **Verb in Base Form (leave)** + **Object (the gate)** + **Complement (open)**.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Voice and Modal Verbs:**

• **Active Structure:** **Subject + Modal + V1 + Object**. For example, **He must finish the work**.

• **Passive Structure:** **Object + Modal + be + V3 + (by + Subject)**. For example, **The work must be finished by him**.

• **Negative Pronouns:** Using **No one** at the beginning of a sentence is more concise and standard than using **Anyone must not...**, which is often considered grammatically weak or non-standard in formal English.

• **Semantic Consistency:** Changing **must** to **should** (as seen in some incorrect options) alters the meaning from a **command/prohibition** to a **suggestion/advice**, which violates the rules of transformation.

• **Verb Tense:** The transformation must maintain the **simple aspect** of the modal; introducing continuous forms like **be leaving** changes the **temporal nature** of the action.

</ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option which can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."
The economic reforms introduced last year are aimed at bringing up the overall productivity of the nation.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**aimed at bringing about**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The verb **aimed** is idiomatically followed by the preposition **at** when expressing a purpose or intention. When **at** is used as a preposition, it must be followed by a **gerund** (the **-ing** form of the verb), making **aimed at bringing** the grammatically correct structure.

• The phrasal verb **bring about** means to **cause something to happen**, to result in, or to initiate a change. In the context of **economic reforms**, the intended goal is to cause an increase or improvement in the **productivity** of the nation.

• The original phrase **bringing up** is contextually inappropriate as it primarily means to **nurture/raise a child** or to **mention a specific topic** during a conversation. It does not collocate with economic metrics like productivity.

• Option 1 is incorrect because **aimed in** is not a standard idiomatic expression for purpose, and **bringing forward** means to move a scheduled event to an **earlier date** or to present a proposal.

• Option 3 is incorrect because while **aim for** can be used with a noun, **aimed at** is the preferred and more formal construction when describing the objective of systemic **reforms** or policies followed by a verb.

 **Additional Information__**

• Understanding Phrasal Verbs with **Bring**:

• **Bring about**: To make something happen, especially a **major change** or **revolution**.

• **Bring up**: To mention a subject or to **rear children**. Example: She was **brought up** in a small town.

• **Bring forward**: To introduce for **discussion** or to change the **timing** of a meeting to an earlier slot.

• **Bring in**: To introduce a **new law**, system, or **legislation**.

• **Bring out**: To **produce** or **launch** a new product, or to highlight a specific **trait**.

</ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
The chairman reaffirmed again his commitment to enhancing the organisation's financial transparency and accountability.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**reaffirmed his commitment**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The verb **reaffirm** is defined as stating or asserting something strongly **once again**. The prefix **re-** in English grammar inherently denotes **repetition** or a return to a previous state.
 
• Using the word **again** in conjunction with **reaffirmed** creates a **pleonasm**, which is the use of more words than are necessary to convey a meaning. This is considered a **redundancy error** in formal writing.
 
• In the original sentence, the phrase **reaffirmed again** essentially translates to **affirmed again again**, which is grammatically incorrect. Removing the word **again** streamlines the sentence and adheres to the rules of **grammatical economy**.
 
• The structure **reaffirmed his commitment** is the most **precise** and **concise** choice, maintaining the **Subject-Verb-Object** flow while effectively conveying that the **chairman** is stating his dedication a second time.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Redundant Phrases in English:**
 
 
• **Option 1 (reaffirmed his commitment again):** Moving the word **again** to the end of the phrase does not eliminate the **semantic overlap**. It remains redundant because the **re-** prefix already carries the meaning of **again**.
 
• **Option 2 (reiterated once again):** The verb **reiterate** means to say something **repeatedly** for emphasis. Combining it with **once again** creates an even more wordy and **redundant** expression than the original sentence.
 
• Common examples of similar errors include **return back**, **revert back**, **recede back**, and **repeat again**. In all these cases, the adverb (back/again) should be omitted for **grammatical correctness**.
 
 
 
• **Contextual Usage:** In **professional communication** and **corporate governance**, using **exact terminology** like **reaffirmed** is preferred to show **consistency** and **transparency** in leadership actions.
</ul

• The passage begins with the time marker '**Last month**', which establishes that the entire narrative is set in the **past tense**. 
• Supporting verbs in the context, such as '**went**' and '**started**', further confirm that the actions occurred in the past. 
• '**Was filled**' is the **Simple Past Passive** form, which is used to describe the state or condition of the atmosphere at that specific time. 
• The other options are incorrect because: 
• '**Fills**' is in the **Simple Present** tense, used for habits or general facts. 
• '**Will fill**' is in the **Future** tense. 
• '**Has filled**' is in the **Present Perfect** tense, which implies a connection to the present. Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 2**'. Complete Passage: *Last month, our class went on an excursion to the National Science Museum. The atmosphere 1. **was filled**__ with excitement as the bus started its journey. Our teacher reminded us to observe carefully and note important details, because the trip was meant to combine fun with learning. As we entered the museum, we saw fascinating models of satellites, robots, and ancient tools. One section 2. __**displayed**__ the history of Indian inventions, from the concept of zero to modern space missions. Everyone listened attentively to the guide, who explained each exhibit with clarity. During the break, a friend said, 'Without science, progress would have been impossible.' Another replied, 'True, but blind dependence on machines 3. __**may**__ lead us into laziness and health problems.' Their discussion showed how science could inspire both admiration and caution. In the afternoon, we attended a workshop on renewable energy. The instructor emphasized that innovation must go hand in hand with responsibility. His words 4. __**served as**__ a reminder that every discovery has consequences, good or bad. On our way back, the teacher concluded, 'The museum visit has not just enriched your knowledge but also encouraged you to think critically. 5. __**Curiosity**__ and responsibility are the pillars of education.'* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 
• The **Passive Voice** (was/were + V3) is often used when the focus is on the state or the recipient of the action rather than the performer. In this case, the focus is on the **atmosphere** being characterized by **excitement**. </ul

questions.question: Which of the following modal verbs correctly fills in blank (C) and completes the sentence?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**may**'. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** __ 
• The sentence is expressing a **possibility** or a **potential consequence** regarding the over-reliance on technology. 
• The modal verb '**may**' is used to indicate that something is possible, even if it is not certain. In this context, it suggests that blind dependence on machines has the potential to lead to laziness and health issues. 
• '**Would**' is typically used for **hypothetical** or **conditional** situations, which is less appropriate here as the speaker is talking about a realistic risk. 
• '**Will**' indicates **certainty** or a definite future outcome, which might be too absolute for a cautionary opinion. 
• '**Shal**' is a misspelling of '**shall**' and is generally used with the first person (I/We) for suggestions or formal future statements. Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 3**'. Complete Passage: *Last month, our class went on an excursion to the National Science Museum. The atmosphere **was filled**__ with excitement as the bus started its journey. Our teacher reminded us to observe carefully and note important details, because the trip was meant to combine fun with learning. As we entered the museum, we saw fascinating models of satellites, robots, and ancient tools. One section __**displayed**__ the history of Indian inventions, from the concept of zero to modern space missions. Everyone listened attentively to the guide, who explained each exhibit with clarity. During the break, a friend said, ‘Without science, progress would have been impossible.’ Another replied, ‘True, but blind dependence on machines __**may**__ lead us into laziness and health problems.’ Their discussion showed how science could inspire both admiration and caution. In the afternoon, we attended a workshop on renewable energy. The instructor emphasized that innovation must go hand in hand with responsibility. His words __**served as**__ a reminder that every discovery has consequences, good or bad. On our way back, the teacher concluded, ‘The museum visit has not just enriched your knowledge but also encouraged you to think critically. __**Curiosity**__ and responsibility are the pillars of education.’* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 
• **Possibility (May/Might/Can)**: Used to express that something could happen. '**May**' is more formal and indicates a medium level of probability. 
• **Necessity/Certainty (Must/Will)**: Used when there is no doubt about the outcome or when something is required. 
• **Hypothetical (Would)**: Used when talking about imaginary or conditional scenarios.

• In this context, the instructor's words functioned as a **reminder** for the students, making '**served as**' the most appropriate choice. Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 1**'. • **Served for**: Usually refers to the duration of time someone worked (e.g., He served for ten years) or a specific purpose, but it does not collocate well with 'a reminder'.
